raw_evidence.label: The Pudding's 2017 driving-time investigation
raw_evidence.content: This dataset powered The Pudding's September 2017 essay 'How far is too far? An analysis of driving times to abortion clinics in the US,' written by data journalists at Polygraph/The Pudding (lead author Russell Goldenberg). The piece reframed abortion access as a driving-time problem rather than a legal one: rather than counting clinics per state or arguing about laws, the team computed round-trip driving times from every contiguous-US city with population over 50,000 to its nearest operating clinic, then re-ran the calculation under the counterfactual that each city's nearest clinic had closed. The four gestation columns (8, 12, 16, 20 weeks) capture the fact that as a pregnancy progresses, fewer clinics will provide care, so the same city can have a one-hour round-trip at 8 weeks and a nine-hour round-trip at 16 weeks. The dataset and headline finding (151 urban areas lack accessible clinics within a one-hour round-trip drive) made the piece an early reference point for how 'access' became operationalized as travel time in journalism.

This is the Pudding's headline number, and it describes a baseline of friction even before any clinic closes.

raw_evidence.label: Average drive triples between 8 and 20 weeks
raw_evidence.content: The population-weighted mean round-trip drive grows from 0.25 hours at 8 weeks to 0.30 at 12, 0.59 at 16, and 1.02 hours at 20 weeks — a 4x increase across the gestational ladder. The share of urban Americans living in a city with a 0-hour drive falls from 88.8% (8 weeks) to 66.9% (20 weeks); the share facing a 4+ hour round-trip rises from 1.4% to 10.8%. Most clinics offer first-trimester care; far fewer perform second-trimester D&E procedures. The clinic universe for a 20-week patient is a small fraction of the universe for an 8-week patient, and the geography of access collapses correspondingly.

sentences.summary: det_03: Why later procedures involve fewer clinics. Source: KFF: gestational limits on abortion (https://www.kff.org/state-health-policy-data/state-indicator/gestational-limit-a) Facts: About 89-91% of US abortions occur before 13 weeks; About 1.3% of US abortions take place after 21 weeks Source: Late termination of pregnancy (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Late_termination_of_pregnancy) Facts: Second-trimester procedures require D&E and additional training; offered by far fewer providers; State-mandated waiting periods often force two-trip schedules

raw_evidence.label: Why later procedures involve fewer clinics
raw_evidence.content: The four gestation columns are not arbitrary intervals — they reflect how the universe of available clinics shrinks as pregnancy progresses. Roughly 89-91% of US abortions occur in the first trimester (before 13 weeks); only about 1.3% take place after 21 weeks. Most clinics offer medical abortion (the pill, generally up to ~10 weeks) or first-trimester surgical abortion. Far fewer offer second-trimester surgical procedures (D&E), which require additional training, equipment, and longer appointments — often spread across two or three days because of state-mandated waiting periods. The result: the city that had a 20-minute drive to its nearest clinic at 8 weeks may have a four-hour drive at 16 weeks because most of the closer clinics simply do not perform later procedures. This is the structural reason that driving-time access collapses for the patients who most need a procedure (later gestations are disproportionately people who discovered the pregnancy late, encountered fetal anomalies, or were delayed by exactly the access barriers this dataset measures).

raw_evidence.label: Abortion deserts (Cartwright et al., 2018)
raw_evidence.content: An ANSIRH/UCSF research team led by Alice Cartwright identified 27 US cities of population >100,000 in early 2017 that did not have a publicly advertised abortion facility within 100 miles — a category they named 'abortion deserts.' The deserts were heavily concentrated in the South and Midwest (15 states represented, with Texas leading at 10 desert cities). The most extreme case in their dataset was Rapid City, South Dakota, where residents had to travel 318 miles to reach a clinic. Cartwright and colleagues published their findings in Contraception in 2018; the methodology overlaps almost exactly with The Pudding's 2017 dataset (50,000+ population cities, distance to nearest clinic) and provides an academic benchmark for the journalism. Both projects converged on the same picture: a striking minority of urban Americans live functionally outside the clinic network, and that minority is geographically clustered.

sentences.summary: det_07: Mandatory waiting periods compound the drive. Source: Guttmacher — Counseling and Waiting Periods for Abortion (https://www.guttmacher.org/state-policy/explore/counseling-and-waiting-periods-a) Facts: 27 states required waiting periods in 2017; 14 states required in-person counseling, forcing two trips

raw_evidence.label: Mandatory waiting periods compound the drive
raw_evidence.content: 27 US states required a mandatory waiting period (typically 18, 24, 48, or 72 hours) between counseling and the procedure as of 2017, and 14 of those required the counseling to be in person — meaning a patient must make two trips to the same clinic. For a patient whose round-trip drive is nine hours, this is not a 'wait'; it is a multi-day expedition that requires lodging, time off work, child care, and (for people of childbearing age, who are disproportionately low-income) often a network of support to cover gas and a hotel. The Pudding's Meridian, Idaho example — a 10-hour round-trip to Utah, two appointments three days apart — is the standard outcome of stacking a long drive on top of a waiting period. Driving time alone understates the burden; the legal calendar attached to that drive is what makes it a genuine barrier.

raw_evidence.label: What 'closest clinic closed' is really modeling
raw_evidence.content: Each gestation column has a sister 'closed' column that recomputes the drive after removing the city's nearest clinic. This is a sensitivity analysis: how fragile is access? The columns let you measure the 'second-clinic gap' — the difference between depending on one clinic versus on two. Cities where this gap is large (e.g. an extra 6+ hours when one clinic disappears) are essentially single-clinic dependent. This was not hypothetical in 2017: Wyoming's only abortion-providing clinic closed in July 2017, leaving the state without one. North Dakota had only one clinic in Fargo. South Dakota's restrictions meant the same. Looking at the closed columns is therefore less of a thought experiment than a dress rehearsal for the closures that were already happening or one law away.

raw_evidence.label: TRAP laws and the Texas closures (HB2 / Whole Woman's Health)
raw_evidence.content: The 2017 dataset captures the system in the immediate aftermath of the most consequential abortion-clinic policy fight of the decade. In 2013 Texas passed HB2, a TRAP (Targeted Restrictions on Abortion Providers) law that required clinics to meet ambulatory-surgical-center standards and required physicians to have hospital admitting privileges within 30 miles. The number of Texas clinics fell from 42 to 19 between November 2013 and October 2015. In June 2016 the Supreme Court struck down those provisions in Whole Woman's Health v. Hellerstedt (5-3), ruling that they imposed an undue burden without medical justification. But the closed clinics did not snap back: by 2017 only a handful had reopened, and Texas drives remained dramatically longer than they had been in 2012. This is why a Pudding map of 2017 driving times reads, in places like West Texas and the Texas/Louisiana borderlands, as a residue of HB2 even after HB2 was overturned. It is also why the dataset's 'what if the closest clinic closed' columns matter — closures rarely happen in isolation, and modeling one clinic's loss is a proxy for what waves of TRAP-driven closures actually did.

raw_evidence.label: Closing the nearest clinic doubles the share of long drives
raw_evidence.content: The dataset's 'closed' columns simulate the closure of the closest clinic — a controlled stress test on the system. The result: the share of cities lacking a 1-hour round-trip jumps from 20.2% to 37.8% at 8 weeks, and from 45.3% to 67.4% at 20 weeks. Population-weighted, the share of urban Americans living in a 0-hour-drive city collapses from 66.9% to 42.7% at 20 weeks. The system is not slack: shutting one clinic per region is enough to push roughly two-thirds of cities outside an hour-round-trip at 20 weeks. This is what the loss of even a single second-trimester provider looks like.

    print(f"{wk}wk\t\t" + "\t".join(f"{p:.1f}%" for p in pcts))

raw_evidence.label: What 'closest clinic closed' is really modeling
raw_evidence.content: Each gestation column has a sister 'closed' column that recomputes the drive after removing the city's nearest clinic. This is a sensitivity analysis: how fragile is access? The columns let you measure the 'second-clinic gap' — the difference between depending on one clinic versus on two. Cities where this gap is large (e.g. an extra 6+ hours when one clinic disappears) are essentially single-clinic dependent. This was not hypothetical in 2017: Wyoming's only abortion-providing clinic closed in July 2017, leaving the state without one. North Dakota had only one clinic in Fargo. South Dakota's restrictions meant the same. Looking at the closed columns is therefore less of a thought experiment than a dress rehearsal for the closures that were already happening or one law away.

raw_evidence.label: TRAP laws and the Texas closures (HB2 / Whole Woman's Health)
raw_evidence.content: The 2017 dataset captures the system in the immediate aftermath of the most consequential abortion-clinic policy fight of the decade. In 2013 Texas passed HB2, a TRAP (Targeted Restrictions on Abortion Providers) law that required clinics to meet ambulatory-surgical-center standards and required physicians to have hospital admitting privileges within 30 miles. The number of Texas clinics fell from 42 to 19 between November 2013 and October 2015. In June 2016 the Supreme Court struck down those provisions in Whole Woman's Health v. Hellerstedt (5-3), ruling that they imposed an undue burden without medical justification. But the closed clinics did not snap back: by 2017 only a handful had reopened, and Texas drives remained dramatically longer than they had been in 2012. This is why a Pudding map of 2017 driving times reads, in places like West Texas and the Texas/Louisiana borderlands, as a residue of HB2 even after HB2 was overturned. It is also why the dataset's 'what if the closest clinic closed' columns matter — closures rarely happen in isolation, and modeling one clinic's loss is a proxy for what waves of TRAP-driven closures actually did.

raw_evidence.label: Why this dataset still matters in the post-Roe era
raw_evidence.content: The 2017 snapshot landed in a specific window: HB2 had just been struck down, but the closed clinics had not reopened. The dataset documents the ground state of the access network just before the Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health (June 2022) decision overturned Roe v. Wade and triggered a wave of total bans and 6/12/15-week bans across roughly half the country. Today many of the cities in this dataset that had a 30-minute round-trip drive in 2017 now have *no* in-state clinic at all — their 2025 round-trip is whatever the drive is to Illinois, New Mexico, Colorado, or Kansas. Reading 2017 numbers in 2026 is a reading of a baseline: the worst-case driving times of 2017 are now the median experience for whole regions of the country. The methodology — bin gestational availability, model nearest-clinic closure — has become standard in the post-Roe access literature.

raw_evidence.label: Distance reduces abortion rate, nonlinearly
raw_evidence.content: A literature stretching back to Joyce, Henshaw and Skatrun has documented that increased driving distance to the nearest abortion provider lowers the abortion rate by 10-31%, with the largest effects from the first 25-100 miles of added distance and diminishing effects after that. Subsequent work — notably exploiting the Texas HB2 closures as a natural experiment — found 'even modest increases in travel distances caused large reductions in abortions, and that the effect of travel distance on abortion rates is nonlinear, with initial increases in distance having the largest effects.' This matters for interpreting The Pudding's data: a city that crosses from a 30-minute round-trip to a four-hour round-trip is not a marginal change. It is the part of the curve where access most rapidly disappears, and it disproportionately affects low-income, uninsured, and rural patients who cannot easily absorb a multi-day trip plus state-mandated waiting periods.

raw_evidence.content: The dataset's 'closed' columns simulate the closure of the closest clinic — a controlled stress test on the system. The result: the share of cities lacking a 1-hour round-trip jumps from 20.2% to 37.8% at 8 weeks, and from 45.3% to 67.4% at 20 weeks. Population-weighted, the share of urban Americans living in a 0-hour-drive city collapses from 66.9% to 42.7% at 20 weeks. The system is not slack: shutting one clinic per region is enough to push roughly two-thirds of cities outside an hour-round-trip at 20 weeks. This is what the loss of even a single second-trimester provider looks like.

raw_evidence.label: Why this dataset still matters in the post-Roe era
raw_evidence.content: The 2017 snapshot landed in a specific window: HB2 had just been struck down, but the closed clinics had not reopened. The dataset documents the ground state of the access network just before the Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health (June 2022) decision overturned Roe v. Wade and triggered a wave of total bans and 6/12/15-week bans across roughly half the country. Today many of the cities in this dataset that had a 30-minute round-trip drive in 2017 now have *no* in-state clinic at all — their 2025 round-trip is whatever the drive is to Illinois, New Mexico, Colorado, or Kansas. Reading 2017 numbers in 2026 is a reading of a baseline: the worst-case driving times of 2017 are now the median experience for whole regions of the country. The methodology — bin gestational availability, model nearest-clinic closure — has become standard in the post-Roe access literature.

raw_evidence.label: Distance reduces abortion rate, nonlinearly
raw_evidence.content: A literature stretching back to Joyce, Henshaw and Skatrun has documented that increased driving distance to the nearest abortion provider lowers the abortion rate by 10-31%, with the largest effects from the first 25-100 miles of added distance and diminishing effects after that. Subsequent work — notably exploiting the Texas HB2 closures as a natural experiment — found 'even modest increases in travel distances caused large reductions in abortions, and that the effect of travel distance on abortion rates is nonlinear, with initial increases in distance having the largest effects.' This matters for interpreting The Pudding's data: a city that crosses from a 30-minute round-trip to a four-hour round-trip is not a marginal change. It is the part of the curve where access most rapidly disappears, and it disproportionately affects low-income, uninsured, and rural patients who cannot easily absorb a multi-day trip plus state-mandated waiting periods.
